title: What Counts as a Mental Disorder
objective: After this level you can explain how clinicians distinguish a mental disorder from ordinary struggles and what the DSM is.
summary: A mental disorder is a significant disturbance in thinking, emotion or behavior, usually with distress or trouble functioning. The DSM classifies disorders, and its line moves with evidence.

cards.headline: Nearly 1 in 7 people worldwide live with a mental disorder.
cards.body: That was the World Health Organization's estimate for 2023: about 1.2 billion people. Yet everyone has bad days, nerves and grief. So where does an ordinary struggle end and a disorder begin?

cards.headline: Unusual isn't enough
cards.body: The World Health Organization describes a mental disorder as a clinically significant disturbance in a person's thinking, emotion regulation or behavior. The American Psychiatric Association adds what usually comes with it: distress, or problems functioning at work, with family or with friends. Being unusual doesn't count on its own; red hair is uncommon, and it isn't a disorder. Neither does an expected reaction. Deep sadness after a loved one dies is grief, not a disorder by itself.

mascot.line: Keep this: a disorder means real distress or trouble functioning, not just being different.

cards.headline: The manual on the shelf
cards.body: Clinicians work from a shared rulebook. In the United States it's the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, or DSM, published by the American Psychiatric Association. The first edition appeared in 1952; the current one, DSM-5-TR, in 2022. Its criteria spell out which symptoms must be present, and for how long. Psychiatrists, psychologists and counselors all use it. Much of the world relies on the World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases, the ICD, for diagnosis.

cards.headline: When evidence moved the line
cards.body: The first DSM, in 1952, listed homosexuality as a disorder. In the late 1950s the psychologist Evelyn Hooker compared gay and straight men who weren't psychiatric patients, and found no more signs of psychological disturbance in the gay men. In 1973 the American Psychiatric Association concluded that disorders regularly bring distress or impairment, that homosexuality itself doesn't, and voted to remove it. The manual is a tool, and tools get corrected.

cards.headline: What counts as a disorder
learned: Disorder: clinically significant disturbance, usually with distress or trouble functioning
Unusual or expected reactions, like grief, aren't enough
The DSM (American Psychiatric Association) and the WHO's ICD classify disorders
In 1973 evidence moved the line on homosexuality

questions.prompt: Which organization publishes the DSM, the manual US clinicians use to classify mental disorders?

options.label: The World Health Organization
options.rationale: The WHO publishes the ICD, not the DSM.

options.label: The American Psychological Association
options.rationale: Same initials as Level 1's APA, but the DSM comes from the psychiatrists.

options.label: The National Institute of Mental Health
options.rationale: NIMH funds research; it doesn't publish the DSM.

questions.explanation: The DSM is published by the American Psychiatric Association; its current edition, DSM-5-TR, came out in 2022.

questions.prompt: Why did the American Psychiatric Association remove homosexuality from the DSM in 1973?

options.label: Disorders bring distress or impairment, and it itself doesn't
Being unusual had become enough to count as a disorder
options.rationale: The reverse: being unusual alone was never enough.

options.label: The World Health Organization ordered the change
options.rationale: The decision was the American Psychiatric Association's own vote.

options.label: The DSM stopped listing any conditions that year
options.rationale: The DSM still lists hundreds of conditions.

questions.explanation: The APA concluded that disorders regularly cause distress or impairment and homosexuality does not; Evelyn Hooker's research had found no more disturbance in gay men.

questions.prompt: Someone's worries have lasted months and now keep them from work. Using Level 2, who could assess whether this meets DSM criteria?

options.label: An industrial-organizational psychologist
options.rationale: They work on workplaces, not on diagnosing disorders.

options.label: A forensic psychologist
options.rationale: They work in the justice system.

options.label: A clinical psychologist or a psychiatrist
A friend with an online checklist
options.rationale: The DSM guides trained professionals, not home quizzes.

questions.explanation: Clinical psychologists diagnose and treat psychological disorders, and psychiatrists also diagnose; both use the DSM.
